source: OneAquaHealth Catalogue of measures for urban aquatic ecosystems rehabilitation (D2.4, Dias, Serra, Feio, 2025)
notes: Page numbers are PDF pages of the Zenodo file. Operational steps that are not Catalogue measures are marked catalogue: false. No measure uses chemical vector control; AquaSentinel does not recommend insecticides.

verification_visit.title: Verification visit: find and remove standing water at the margins
verification_visit.detail: A city or public health technician confirms the volunteer reports, maps standing pools and removes small breeding sites (blocked grates, containers). No insecticides.

veterinary_notification.title: Notify the veterinary team about dead birds
veterinary_notification.detail: Forward the dead-bird reports (count, place, time, photo taken without touching) to the regional veterinary service, which decides whether to collect and test. AquaSentinel makes no diagnosis.

M4.3.1.title: Remove obsolete barriers (weirs) that hold stagnant water
M4.3.1.quote: during drought periods, low-head barriers may retain stagnant water, providing favourable conditions for mosquito breeding

M4.1.2.title: Active riparian vegetation restoration
M4.1.2.note: Policy Brief p.7: keeping insectivorous birds in cities through riparian vegetation and less light at night may help regulate disease vectors.

M4.6.1.title: Rain gardens
M4.6.1.mosquito_warning: The Catalogue warns that poorly drained rain gardens can create stagnant water pockets that support mosquito larvae; it asks for well-draining substrate, no standing water for more than 48 hours, and regular maintenance.

M4.6.6.title: Vegetated swales
M4.6.6.mosquito_warning: The Catalogue warns that poorly designed or unmaintained swales may retain stagnant water, leading to mosquito breeding.

M4.6.7.title: Retention ponds and floodable parks
M4.6.7.mosquito_warning: The Catalogue warns that poorly designed or unmaintained ponds may retain stagnant water, leading to mosquito breeding.
